subject: economics
title: Environment and Sustainable Development
meta: Lesson practice set · Question types of the April 2026 NIOS paper
instructions: Practice set for this lesson in the question types of the April 2026 paper.

Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match, one word or complete the table).

questions.q: State True or False: (a) Living things are abiotic. (b) Non-living things are abiotic.
questions.answer:
(a) False — living things are biotic.
(b) True.

questions.q: State True or False: (a) Sustainable development is a long-term concept. (b) Consumption should not be restrained to basic needs.
questions.answer:
(a) True.
(b) False — to reduce, consumption should be restrained to basic needs.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) We should find ______ for non-renewable resources. (b) We should use renewable resources ______.
questions.answer:
(a) substitutes
(b) judiciously (efficiently)

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) The environment includes ______ and abiotic factors. (b) Water pollution affects the ______ of water.
questions.answer:
(a) biotic
(b) chemistry (quality)

questions.q: Give one word: (a) A resource that gets replenished over time. (b) Reusing rainwater collected from roofs.
questions.answer:
(a) Renewable resource.
(b) Rainwater harvesting.

questions.q: Name: (a) Two natural sources of air pollution. (b) Two diseases caused by polluted water.
questions.answer:
(a) Dust from barren land, wildfires, volcanoes, methane from cattle (any two).
(b) Cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea (any two).

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Name two kinds of environmental degradation.
questions.answer:
(1) Soil degradation — loss of soil quality and fertility.
(2) Habitat degradation — loss of a habitat's ability to support native life.

questions.q: What are the effects of air pollution?
questions.answer: Difficulty in breathing, coughing and wheezing; aggravation of heart and lung disease; more hospital visits and premature death — about 2.4 million deaths a year worldwide (WHO).

questions.q: What is resource depletion?
questions.answer: Resource depletion is the exhaustion of raw materials in an area through over-use in farming, fishing and mining, e.g. petroleum, coal, natural gas and gold becoming scarce.

questions.q: What is water pollution? Name two sources.
questions.answer:
Water pollution is the contamination of rivers, lakes, seas and groundwater by untreated wastes.
Sources: sewage from towns, industrial effluents, farm runoff of pesticides and fertilisers, oil spills.

questions.q: 'The environment sustains life through biodiversity.' Explain.
questions.answer: The environment supports a variety of life forms, which adapt, evolve and depend on each other and on air, water and soil. Preserving the environment preserves this biodiversity and life itself.

or.q: 'Pollution harms the health of living beings.' Explain.
or.answer: Polluted air causes breathing and heart problems; polluted water causes cholera and typhoid and kills fish; noise causes stress and hearing loss. So pollution harms the health of humans, animals and plants.

questions.q: How does recycling help sustainable development?
questions.answer: Recycling means using things again. Recycling paper saves trees, since paper is made from wood pulp, and rainwater harvesting saves scarce water, so resources last for future generations.

or.q: What is meant by judicious use of resources?
or.answer: Using resources carefully and only as needed — avoiding waste, using renewable resources at a rate they can renew, and replacing non-renewables with solar, wind and biogas.

questions.q: How does the environment absorb harmful wastes?
questions.answer: Smoke from chimneys and vehicles, sewage and industrial effluents are absorbed by air, water and soil, and are cleaned and recycled by natural processes — as long as they are within its capacity.

questions.q: Suggest two steps a farmer can take to reduce soil degradation.
questions.answer:
(1) Use chemical fertilisers and pesticides sparingly and use organic manure.
(2) Avoid over-irrigation (and drain fields) and prevent overgrazing by keeping plant cover.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain the sources of air pollution.
questions.answer:
Man-made: smoke from power plants and factories, exhaust from vehicles, farm chemicals and dust, fumes of paint and aerosol sprays, and methane from landfills.
Natural: dust from barren land, methane from cattle digestion, smoke from wildfires, and gases and ash from volcanoes.

questions.q: What are the causes of habitat degradation?
questions.answer:
(1) Deforestation and wood extraction for timber.
(2) Conversion of forest land into farmland.
(3) Urban expansion into natural habitats.
(4) Soil erosion and desertification.
(5) Slash-and-burn agriculture.

questions.q: 'Habitat degradation reduces the carrying capacity of an area.' Explain.
questions.answer:
Carrying capacity is the number of plants and animals of a species an area can support.
When forests are cut and land is cleared, food and shelter are lost, so fewer animals and plants can survive there.
Populations fall, food chains are upset, and species may become extinct.

questions.q: Distinguish between renewable and non-renewable resources with examples.
questions.answer:
Renewable resources are replenished naturally over time and can be used without running out if used carefully — forests, fish, water, solar and wind energy.
Non-renewable resources are exhausted as they are used and cannot be replaced — coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals. They must be used carefully for future generations.

questions.q: What is noise pollution? What are its effects?
questions.answer:
Noise pollution is excessive, displeasing noise from traffic, industry, construction and appliances.
Effects: annoyance and aggression, stress, hypertension, sleep disturbance, heart problems and noise-induced hearing loss.

questions.q: What is meant by soil degradation? State its causes.
questions.answer:
Soil degradation is an undesirable change in soil quality: it loses nutrients and humus and becomes unfit for crops.
Causes: excessive chemical fertilisers and pesticides; waterlogging from over-irrigation; overgrazing, which leads to erosion.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: How can we contribute to sustainable development?
questions.answer:
Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs, and we must see the world as a whole.
(1) Resources: find substitutes for non-renewable resources — solar cookers and lanterns, windmills, hydro, tidal power and gobar gas — and use renewable resources judiciously.
(2) Recycle: recycle paper to save trees, and harvest rainwater.
(3) Reduce: restrain consumption to basic needs — walk instead of driving, use the stairs, switch off unneeded fans and lights.
Governments and international bodies must also coordinate policy, since pollution crosses borders.

questions.q: What is air pollution? State four natural sources and two effects.
questions.answer:
Air pollution is the introduction into the atmosphere of chemicals, particles or biological matter that harm living beings or the environment, e.g. sulphur and nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and particulates.
Natural sources: (1) dust from barren land; (2) methane from cattle; (3) smoke and carbon monoxide from wildfires; (4) sulphur, chlorine and ash from volcanoes.
Effects: (1) breathing difficulty, coughing and aggravated heart and lung disease; (2) more hospital admissions and premature deaths (2.4 million a year, WHO). Carbon dioxide also adds to global warming.

questions.q: What is habitat degradation? Mention two causes and one effect.
questions.answer:
Habitat degradation is the process by which a habitat loses its ability to support native life because of human activities, which reduces its carrying capacity.
Causes: (1) deforestation and timber extraction; (2) conversion of forests to farmland and urban expansion (also slash-and-burn farming and desertification).
Effect: loss of biodiversity and extinction of species, which upsets food chains. It also makes the area more prone to floods, droughts and crop failure.

questions.q: Explain three major causes of soil degradation.
questions.answer:
(1) Excessive use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides makes the soil acidic, saline or alkaline, reduces humus, and adds toxins and heavy metals such as cadmium and lead.
(2) Waterlogging: over-irrigation without drainage raises the salt content, making soil unfit for crops and breeding mosquitoes.
(3) Overgrazing by animals removes plant cover and leaves the soil open to erosion.
Result: lower yields, polluted groundwater, loss of biodiversity and desertification.

questions.q: Explain the significance of the environment.
questions.answer:
(1) It provides renewable resources (forests, fish) and non-renewable resources (coal, petroleum).
(2) It absorbs and recycles wastes such as smoke, sewage and effluents.
(3) It sustains life through biodiversity.
(4) It has aesthetic value — scenery and landscapes that are part of human culture.
